opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing academia has to be honest about is that we're not going to win a compute race against OpenAI or any of the big labs. If your research direction is basically "train a bigger model than everyone else," that's not a good choice for a university group. So the question becomes: what can academia do that companies either can't do, or won't do because it's not on their critical path?

One answer is to work on things that are a few steps ahead of where industry is focused. Companies are under real pressure to ship products, so they tend to concentrate on what's going to matter in the next six months to a year. Academia can afford to explore ideas that might look strange or impractical today but become important two or three years later. Reinforcement learning for language models is a good example. For a long time people treated RL as something niche, mostly for games or robotics. But if you'd been working seriously on RL algorithms, reward design, multi-agent systems, those turned out to be exactly the skills that became central once reasoning models took off.

The second answer is to do work that's open and reproducible. A lot of the frontier labs don't publish the details anymore. So there's real value in academia building open frameworks, open recipes, and systems that the whole community can use and verify. When we worked on RL training infrastructure, part of the motivation was simply that if nobody outside the big companies knows how to do large-scale RL training efficiently, then the rest of the field can't even participate in the conversation.

The third answer is about understanding, not just performance. Companies care whether something works. Academia should also care about why it works, when it fails, and what the underlying principles are. That kind of scientific understanding often gets skipped in industry because there isn't time, but it's what makes progress sustainable.

And finally, I'd say don't be afraid to collaborate with industry. It doesn't have to be academia versus companies. Students often go back and forth, and some of the best work comes from people who understand both the real-world constraints and the longer-term research questions. The key is that academics should pick problems where their particular advantages, freedom, patience, openness, really matter, rather than trying to imitate what a big lab does with a hundredth of the resources.

r001.rationale: The response recommends exploring ideas that may seem strange or impractical today and could matter later, which communicates pursuing non-consensus research.

r002.rationale: It advises against trying to beat OpenAI and other labs in the compute race or imitating their near-term product focus, and recommends choosing problems outside their likely priorities.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think the first thing to be honest about is that academia simply cannot compete with OpenAI on their own terms. If the game is "train the biggest model with the most compute and the most data," a university lab loses before it starts. We don't have ten thousand GPUs, we don't have a hundred-person infrastructure team, and we can't spend a year on one training run. So if a professor says "my goal is to build a better GPT," I'd gently suggest that's not a research direction, that's a wish.

But I actually think this is liberating rather than depressing. Companies have very specific constraints. They have to ship products, they have to show results on a quarterly timescale, and they're pushed toward whatever scales right now. That means there's a lot of territory they will systematically under-explore. Academia's job is to go to exactly those places.

Concretely, I see a few kinds of questions that fit universities well. One is understanding, not building. Why does in-context learning work? What is actually happening when you do RLHF? What are the failure modes, and can we characterize them? A company will care about these questions only to the extent they help the next release. A university can care about them because they're true or false.

The second is working at small scale deliberately, with the goal of finding things that will matter at large scale. Many of the ideas that ended up in today's big models started as small experiments. Things like better optimization, new training objectives, data selection, agents and multi-agent interaction, reinforcement learning algorithms. You can study these with a handful of GPUs if you design the experiments well. The key is to ask: is this phenomenon likely to persist as we scale up, or is it an artifact of being small? That's a scientific skill, and academia is good at it.

The third is the long tail of problems with no obvious product. Robotics is a good example. Game-theoretic settings, cooperation among agents, safety and alignment questions that are hard to measure. These are areas where a company might fund a team for a while and then cut it when priorities shift. A professor can stay on a problem for ten years.

And honestly, the last thing I'd say is about people. Academia's most important output is not papers, it's students. The people who are now leading these labs at OpenAI, DeepMind, Anthropic and so on were trained at universities. If we train people who understand the fundamentals deeply and can think independently, rather than just reproducing the current trend, that's a contribution no company can replace.

So my summary would be: don't chase OpenAI, complement them. Ask the questions they can't afford to ask, work on the problems they're not incentivized to work on, and train the people who will eventually push the whole field forward, whether that's inside industry or outside it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends pursuing areas companies systematically under-explore, including long-term problems without obvious products and questions that industry is not incentivized to ask.

r002.rationale: It says academia cannot compete with OpenAI at training the biggest models, advises against trying to build a better GPT, and summarizes the strategy as “don’t chase OpenAI, complement them.”

astra-6.text:
I think academia should be aware of what companies like OpenAI are doing, but it shouldn’t simply follow their roadmap. If a company has far more compute, data, and engineering resources, trying to compete on exactly the same problem may not be the best use of a university lab.

Academia has the freedom to ask questions that don’t have an immediate commercial payoff. Can we learn more efficiently? Can we understand why a method works and where it fails? Are there alternative approaches that look unpromising today but could become important in five or ten years?

That doesn’t mean avoiding problems that industry works on. The distinction is whether we have an independent scientific question and a meaningful way to investigate it. A small, carefully designed experiment can teach us something that scaling up alone won’t reveal.

So I would treat industry’s progress as useful evidence, rather than as the agenda. Universities should help expand the set of possibilities, while training students to identify important problems and think independently.

r001.rationale: It says academia can explore alternative approaches that may seem unpromising today and should expand the set of possibilities.

r002.rationale: It advises against simply following industry’s roadmap or competing on the same problem, but does not specifically say to avoid directions OpenAI will predictably pursue; it allows work on problems industry also works on when there is an independent scientific question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think academia should avoid simply following whatever OpenAI is doing. Companies have advantages in computing resources, data, and engineering, so if a university lab tries to compete on exactly the same terms, it’s going to be very difficult.

But academia has the freedom to ask questions that don’t have an immediate commercial return. We can investigate why these systems work, where they fail, and whether there are fundamentally different approaches worth exploring. We can also pursue smaller, carefully controlled experiments that help distinguish a real scientific advance from the effect of adding more compute.

That doesn’t mean ignoring industry. What companies achieve can reveal important research questions. But we should choose directions based on what we can uniquely contribute and what will remain scientifically valuable, rather than just chasing the latest product announcement.

r001.rationale: The response recommends exploring questions and fundamentally different approaches beyond commercially driven work, rather than merely following industry priorities.

r002.rationale: It says academia should avoid simply following what OpenAI is doing and competing on the same terms, which communicates avoiding directions industry is likely to pursue.
